39|BACKGROUND
40|Androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) has been the backbone of treatment for
41|metastatic prostate cancer since the 1940s. We assessed whether concomitant
42|treatment with ADT plus docetaxel would result in longer overall survival than that
43|with ADT alone.
44|METHODS
45|We assigned men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer to receive
46|either ADT plus docetaxel (at a dose of 75 mg per square meter of body-surface
47|area every 3 weeks for six cycles) or ADT alone. The primary objective was to test
48|the hypothesis that the median overall survival would be 33.3% longer among
49|patients receiving docetaxel added to ADT early during therapy than among pa-
50|tients receiving ADT alone.
51|RESULTS
52|A total of 790 patients (median age, 63 years) underwent randomization. After a
53|median follow-up of 28.9 months, the median overall survival was 13.6 months
54|longer with ADT plus docetaxel (combination therapy) than with ADT alone (57.6
55|months vs. 44.0 months; hazard ratio for death in the combination group, 0.61;
56|95% confidence interval [CI], 0.47 to 0.80; P<0.001). The median time to bio-
57|chemical, symptomatic, or radiographic progression was 20.2 months in the com-
58|bination group, as compared with 11.7 months in the ADT-alone group (hazard
59|ratio, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.72; P<0.001). The rate of a prostate-specific antigen
60|level of less than 0.2 ng per milliliter at 12 months was 27.7% in the combination
61|group versus 16.8% in the ADT-alone group (P<0.001). In the combination group,
62|the rate of grade 3 or 4 febrile neutropenia was 6.2%, the rate of grade 3 or 4
63|infection with neutropenia was 2.3%, and the rate of grade 3 sensory neuropathy
64|and of grade 3 motor neuropathy was 0.5%.
65|CONCLUSIONS
66|Six cycles of docetaxel at the beginning of ADT for metastatic prostate cancer re-
67|sulted in significantly longer overall survival than that with ADT alone. (Funded by
68|the National Cancer Institute and others; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00309985.)

6|cancer were first documented in the 1940s
7|and were achieved with surgical castra-
8|tion; subsequently, androgen-deprivation therapy
9|(ADT) became the mainstay of therapy.1 Attempts
10|to improve the efficacy or decrease the treatment
11|burden of ADT have included the use of anti
12|androgens alone, intermittent dosing of ADT,
13|and the use of an antiandrogen combined with
14|medical or surgical castration.2-4 A meta-analysis
15|revealed an increase in survival of 3 percentage
16|points at 5 years with concurrent use of a non-
17|steroidal antiandrogen at the time of initiation
18|of ADT.2 However, resistance to ADT occurs in
19|most patients, with the result that the median
20|survival among patients with metastatic prostate
21|cancer is approximately 3 years.5,6 In patients
22|with resistance to ADT, docetaxel therapy re-
23|sulted in a median survival that was approxi-
24|mately 2.5 months longer than that with mito-
25|xantrone and prednisone.7,8
26|Prior studies of chemotherapy plus ADT, which
27|did not show a benefit, were small studies that
28|involved primarily patients with a relatively low
29|tumor burden.9,10 Definitions of a high burden of
30|disease have included the presence of visceral
31|metastases, a bone-metastasis burden categorized
32|by site (beyond the axial skeleton) or by a high
33|number of lesions, or a combination of these.9,11,12
34|In this study, the E3805 study, patients received
35|ADT alone or ADT plus docetaxel at the begin-
36|ning of ADT for metastatic hormone-sensitive
37|prostate cancer, and stratification was performed
38|prospectively according to high or low burden of
39|metastatic disease.
40|Methods
41|Study Oversight
42|The primary objective of the E3805 study was to
43|determine whether docetaxel therapy at the be-
44|ginning of ADT for metastatic hormone-sensitive
45|prostate cancer would result in longer overall
46|survival than that with ADT alone. The study was
47|designed in 2005 by the Eastern Cooperative On-
48|cology Group (ECOG; now part of ECOG-ACRIN)
49|and was approved by the institutional review
50|board at each participating institution. The study
51|was coordinated by the ECOG-ACRIN Cancer
52|Research Group. The ECOG-ACRIN Statistical
53|Center collected the data and was the leading
54|cooperative group and data coordinating center.
55|The first two authors attest that the study was
56|conducted and monitored as specified by the
57|protocol. The first author wrote the first draft of
58|the manuscript, with subsequent contributions
59|by all the coauthors. The authors vouch for the
60|accuracy and completeness of the data presented.
61|The protocol with the statistical analysis plan
62|is available with the full text of this article at
63|NEJM.org. Sanofi donated the docetaxel for
64|early use (i.e., before progression during ADT)
65|and provided a grant to ECOG-ACRIN but had
66|no role in the design of the protocol, the collec-
67|tion or analysis of the data, or the preparation of
68|the manuscript.
69|Patients
70|Patients were enrolled by ECOG-ACRIN, the
71|Southwest Oncology Group, the Alliance for
72|Clinical Trials in Oncology, and NRG Oncology
73|(a merged group that includes the National Sur-
74|gical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project, the Ra-
75|diation Therapy Oncology Group, and the Gyne-
76|cologic Oncology Group) and through the Clinical
77|Trials Support Unit. Eligible patients had a
78|pathological diagnosis of prostate cancer or a
79|clinical scenario consistent with prostate cancer
80|with an elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
81|level; radiologic evidence of metastatic disease;
82|and an ECOG performance-status score of 0, 1,
83|or 2 (on a scale from 0 to 5, with higher scores
84|indicating greater disability; patients with a score
85|of 2 were eligible if the decrement in function-
86|ing was due to prostate cancer). Prior adjuvant
87|ADT was allowed if the duration of therapy was
88|24 months or less and progression had occurred
89|more than 12 months after completion of ther-
90|apy. Patients who were receiving ADT for meta-
91|static disease were eligible if there was no evidence
92|of progression and treatment had commenced
93|within 120 days before randomization. Organ
94|function that was adequate for docetaxel treat-
95|ment was required (details are provided in the
96|protocol). All patients provided written informed
97|consent in accordance with institutional and
98|federal guidelines.
99|Treatment Plan, Stratification,
100|and Randomization

102|or to combination therapy with ADT plus doce

18|visceral metastases or ≥4 bone lesions with ≥1
19|beyond the vertebral bodies and pelvis] vs. low
20|volume). Patients were required to take at least
21|500 mg of oral calcium carbonate and at least
22|400 IU of vitamin D per day.
23|Dose Modifications
24|No dose modifications of ADT were allowed,
25|and the use of a nonsteroidal antiandrogen with
26|castration (medical or surgical) at the time of
27|initiation of therapy was at the discretion of the
28|investigator. Intermittent hormonal therapy was
29|not allowed. For docetaxel, no more than two
30|dose modifications (decreases to 65 mg per
31|square meter and 55 mg per square meter) were
32|allowed. Dose adjustments were made according
33|to the organ system that showed the greatest de-
34|gree of toxic effects, which were graded accord-
35|ing to the National Cancer Institute (NCI) Com-
36|mon Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events
37|(CTCAE; version 3.0 until September 2011 and
38|version 4.0 thereafter). Details on dosing are
39|provided in the protocol. If a dose was reduced
40|owing to toxic effects, it was not increased sub-
41|sequently, and docetaxel was discontinued if
42|administration was delayed longer than 3 weeks
43|from the scheduled day of dosing. The use of
44|growth factors was at the discretion of the inves-
45|tigator.
46|Monitoring of Toxic Effects and Efficacy
47|Patients assigned to combination therapy were
48|seen every 3 weeks during the period of docetaxel
49|administration and then every 3 months. Patients
50|assigned to ADT alone were seen every 3 months.
51|For the reporting of serious adverse events to the
52|NCI and to guide dose modifications, CTCAE
53|version 3.0 was used until September 2011, at
54|which time the study began using version 4.0. To
55|ensure consistency, case-report forms for toxic
56|effects that were recorded in the study database
57|retained the use of version 3.0. All grade 3 or
58|higher toxic effects in the combination group
59|were captured, and an attribution of relatedness
60|to study therapy was made by the local investiga-
61|tors. Adverse events among patients assigned to
62|ADT alone were not routinely documented, al-
63|though major adverse events were to be reported.
64|PSA levels were measured at each scheduled
65|visit. Imaging (computed tomography [CT] of
66|the abdomen and pelvis, technetium-99m bone
67|scanning, and radiography or CT of the chest)
68|was performed at baseline and at the time of
69|documented castration resistance or as clinically
70|indicated. Disease progression on imaging was
71|determined according to the Response Evaluation
72|Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), version 1.013
73|(the criteria are summarized in the protocol). A
74|complete serologic response was defined as a
75|PSA level of less than 0.2 ng per milliliter on two
76|consecutive measurements at least 4 weeks apart.
77|Serologic progression was defined as an increase
78|in the PSA level of more than 50% above the
79|nadir reached after the initiation of ADT, with
80|two consecutive increases at least 2 weeks apart.
81|The date of a first recorded increase of more
82|than 50% above the nadir was deemed the date
83|of progression. If the nadir level was less than
84|2 ng per milliliter, a minimum increase of more
85|than 2 ng per milliliter was required.
86|All time-to-event end points were determined
87|from the time of randomization. Overall survival
88|was defined as the time until death from any
89|cause. The time to castration-resistant prostate
90|cancer was defined as the time until document-
91|ed clinical or serologic progression with a testos-
92|terone level of less than 50 ng per deciliter (or
93|source documentation of medical castration or
94|surgical castration). The time to clinical pro-
95|gression was defined as the time until increas-
96|ing symptoms of bone metastases; progression
97|according to RECIST, version 1.0; or clinical
98|deterioration due to cancer according to the in-
99|vestigator's opinion.

Blinding participants, most commonly through use of a placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences. If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether participants were aware of their assigned intervention during the trial.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when participants knew their assignment, including when intervention-specific side effects or toxicities revealed it. Blinding participants, commonly with placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences.
evidence_needed: A direct report of participant blinding, open-label conduct, or participant knowledge during the trial.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an absent explicit awareness statement alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment.

answer_anchors.text: Participants were aware of their assigned intervention.
Participants were blinded to their assigned intervention.

considerations: Awareness is about knowledge of assignment, not whether participants completed or received treatment.

questions.wording: Were carers and people delivering the interventions aware of participants' assigned intervention during the trial?
questions.official_guidance: If carers or people delivering the interventions are aware of the assigned intervention then its implementation, or administration of non-protocol interventions, may differ between the intervention groups. Blinding may prevent such differences. If randomized allocation was not concealed, then it is likely that carers and people delivering the interventions were aware of participants’ assigned intervention during the trial.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.2
questions.bias_construct: Whether carers and people delivering interventions were aware of participants' assigned intervention.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when carers or intervention personnel knew assignment, including when participant side effects or toxicities revealed it. If randomized allocation was not concealed, awareness by carers and delivery personnel is likely.
evidence_needed: A direct report of blinding or awareness by carers and people delivering the intervention, plus the allocation process when it bears on their awareness.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when awareness of carers or delivery personnel cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: Carers or intervention personnel were aware of assigned intervention.
Carers or intervention personnel were blinded to assigned intervention.

considerations: Assess the people delivering interventions, not merely outcome assessors.

questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2: Were there deviations from the intended intervention that arose because of the trial context?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe, that the trial context led to failure to implement the protocol interventions or to implementation of interventions not allowed by the protocol. Answer ‘No’ or ‘Probably no’ if there were changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol, such as non-adherence to intervention, but these are consistent with what could occur outside the trial context. The answer ‘No information’ may be appropriate.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.3
questions.bias_construct: Whether deviations inconsistent with protocol arose because of the trial context.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes only after establishing both that the change was inconsistent with the protocol and that the trial context caused it; identify both premises in the justification. Answer no or probably no when no such deviation occurred, including ordinary non-adherence outside the trial context, protocol-consistent changes, and protocol-permitted subsequent care after progression.
evidence_needed: Evidence linking the deviation to recruitment, engagement, or trial personnel and showing it was inconsistent with the protocol.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when reported details are insufficient and trial circumstances do not support a reasonable probable judgment about trial-context-caused deviations.

answer_anchors.text: The trial context caused protocol-inconsistent deviations.
No protocol-inconsistent deviation arose because of the trial context.
Reported details and trial circumstances do not support a judgment about trial-context-caused deviations.

considerations: Side-effect-related compromised blinding counts only when resulting changes were protocol-inconsistent and context-caused.

Subsequent treatment, rescue treatment, or cross-over is not itself a deviation for the effect of assignment: establish both protocol inconsistency and a trial-context cause before answering affirmatively.
invalid_shortcuts: unequal post-progression treatment without evidence that it was prohibited and trial-context-caused
a protocol deviation without its cause

questions.wording: If Y/PY to 2.3: Were these deviations likely to have affected the outcome?
questions.official_guidance: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context will impact on the intervention effect estimate if they affect the outcome, but not otherwise.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.4
questions.bias_construct: Whether context-caused protocol-inconsistent deviations were likely to affect the outcome.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the identified deviations were likely to affect the intervention effect estimate through this outcome; answer no or probably no when they were not likely to affect the outcome.
evidence_needed: A direct link between the identified context-caused deviation and this outcome or its effect estimate.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the effect of the identified deviations on the outcome cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The identified deviations were likely to affect the outcome.
The identified deviations were not likely to affect the outcome.

considerations: This question concerns the deviations already identified in 2.3, not any non-adherence in isolation.

questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 2.4: Were these deviations from intended intervention balanced between groups?
questions.official_guidance: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context are more likely to impact on intervention effect estimate if they are not balanced between the intervention groups.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.5
questions.bias_construct: Whether context-caused protocol-inconsistent deviations were balanced between intervention groups.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the identified deviations were balanced between groups; answer no or probably no when they were not balanced.
evidence_needed: Group-specific counts or descriptions of the identified deviations and their comparability between intervention groups.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when balance of the identified deviations cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The identified deviations were balanced between intervention groups.
The identified deviations were not balanced between intervention groups.

considerations: Balance refers to the deviations identified in 2.3 and their potential effect, not to baseline group sizes.

questions.wording: Was an appropriate analysis used to estimate the effect of assignment to intervention?
questions.official_guidance: Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate. Both naïve ‘per-protocol’ analyses and ‘as treated’ analyses should be considered inappropriate. Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.6
questions.bias_construct: Whether an appropriate analysis estimated the effect of assignment to intervention. Compare randomized assignment with the actual analysis population, grouping, reassignment, and exclusions, including their reasons; an ITT, modified ITT, or as-treated label alone does not establish this.
questions.decision_rule: Consider ITT and modified ITT excluding participants with missing outcome data appropriate. Consider naive per-protocol, as-treated, and post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants inappropriate; post-randomization exclusion of ineligible participants may be appropriate when eligibility could not have been influenced by assignment.
evidence_needed: The actual analysis population and grouping rule: who was assigned, who was analysed in each group, who was excluded or reassigned after randomization, and why.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an incomplete analysis description alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment about appropriateness.

answer_anchors.text: An ITT or appropriate modified ITT analysis estimated assignment effect.
A naive per-protocol, as-treated, or inappropriate post-randomization exclusion analysis was used.

considerations: The question is about effect of assignment, so grouping must follow randomized assignment.
Assess what the analysis actually did, not the label attached to it: ITT/mITT/as-treated terminology is a description to verify against assignment, grouping, and exclusions.

Never-treated participants are not automatically participants with no adverse event or unavailable outcome. Recover the documented eligibility, outcome availability, and exclusion reason before judging the approved assignment-effect estimand.
invalid_shortcuts: an ITT label without its population
a per-protocol label without the analysis population

questions.wording: If N/PN/NI to 2.6: Was there potential for a substantial impact (on the result) of the failure to analyse participants in the group to which they were randomized?
questions.official_guidance: This question addresses whether the number of participants who were analysed in the wrong intervention group, or excluded from the analysis, was sufficient that there could have been a substantial impact on the result. It is not possible to specify a precise rule: there may be potential for substantial impact even if fewer than 5% of participants were analysed in the wrong group or excluded, if the outcome is rare or if exclusions are strongly related to prognostic factors.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.7
questions.bias_construct: Whether failure to analyse participants in their randomized group could substantially affect the result.
questions.decision_rule: Assess whether the number analysed in the wrong group or excluded was sufficient for substantial impact. There is no precise percentage rule: fewer than 5% may still matter for rare outcomes or exclusions strongly related to prognostic factors.
evidence_needed: Counts and reasons for participants analysed in the wrong group or excluded, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance of exclusions.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the potential magnitude of impact cannot be assessed.

answer_anchors.text: The wrong-group analysis or exclusions could substantially affect the result.
The wrong-group analysis or exclusions could not substantially affect the result.

considerations: This is conditional on an inappropriate or uncertain analysis in 2.6.
Assess potential impact only after deciding whether 2.6 was appropriate; a small or balanced exclusion can have low impact without making an inappropriate analysis appropriate.
invalid_shortcuts: a group label without exclusion counts

sections.excerpt: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.

sections.excerpt: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.3
sections.excerpt: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. sections.excerpt: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness could depend on its true value and (ii) it is likely that missingness depended on its true value. response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

53% information for the efficacy analysis. Pre-specified criteria for significance were reached, and the
Data Monitoring Committee released the data for presentation. Once this decision was made, the study
had essentially achieved "full" information, so the data was finalized soon thereafter in terms of the
primary endpoint. This report thus represents data with a cutoff for survival of December 23, 2013. No
further updates were made in order to preserve the Type I error. Data cleaning continued for other
aspects of the study, including treatment, adverse events, and secondary endpoints. All other data in this
report apart from survival reflect the database as of December 23, 2014.

The primary endpoint of this study is overall survival. The study population consists of prostate cancer
patients with extensive metastatic disease (high volume disease). Patients were stratified based on age
(≥70 versus <70), performance status (0-1 versus 2), prior adjuvant hormonal therapy (>12 months versus
≤12 months), intended use of combined androgen blockade >30 days from start of treatment, and
bisphosphonate use (bisphosphonate was then changed to "FDA approved drugs for delaying skeletal
related events" in addendum 5).

ablation arm (Arm B) by the log-rank test. This study was designed to detect a 33.3% improvement in

therapy arm, corresponding to a hazard ratio of 1.33, with one-sided Type I error of 0.025. Planned full
information was 408 deaths, which provided 80% power, allowing for the interim analysis schedule
